Description

Cd, Hg, and their compounds are formally designated as Specified 
Class I Chemical Substances. Manufacturers, importers, and down-
stream users of such substances shall comply with the Notification 
Obligations.
Cd, Pb, Hg, and their inorganic/organic compounds are regulated as 
hazardous substances, primarily generated through anthropogenic 
emissions arising from combustion, industrial synthesis, or thermal 
decomposition processes.
Enterprises engaged in activities involving hazardous substances shall 
adopt Best Available Techniques (BAT) to reduce emissions.

The production of any Hg-containing batteries is prohibited, with the 
following exceptions:
(a) Zinc silver oxide button cells containing Hg at less than 1% by 
weight.
(b) Zinc air button cells containing Hg at less than 2% by weight.
The use of Hg, Cd, and Pb in electrical and electronic products shall 
comply with the following concentration limits by weight in homoge-
neous materials:
(a) Hg ≤ 0.1% (1,000 ppm)
(b) Cd ≤ 0.01% (100 ppm)
(c) Pb ≤ 0.1% (1,000 ppm)

Products containing Cd, Pb, Hg, or their compounds shall be subject 
to restrictions on sales, custody, storage, transportation, and use, with 
the following concentration thresholds:
(a) Hg ≤ 0.1% (1,000 ppm)
(b) Cd ≤ 0.01% (100 ppm)
(c) Pb ≤ 0.1% (1,000 ppm)

Cd, Hg, and Pb are classified as “Substances with Severe Hazard to 
Waters” (WGK Category 3).

3.1.1  Solvothermal preparation of inp QDs

The  solvothermal  method  represents  an  efficient  and  rapid  approach  for  synthesizing 
highly  crystalline  and  monodisperse  InP  QDs.  This  synthetic  route  involves  the  intro-
duction of precursor mixtures into a solvent maintained at a specific temperature under 
an inert gas atmosphere, facilitating the instantaneous crystallization of InP monomers 
into core structures. This method offers precise control over QDs size, thereby enabling 
effective  bandgap  engineering.  However,  the  method  requires  high  temperature  and 
Pressure confined system (usually > 300 °C, > 10 MPa), which increases the risk of explo-
sion and the difficulty of safe operation. And its solvent and precursor toxicity will cause 
a certain burden on the environment. As demonstrated by Sarma et al., the solvothermal 
synthesis route successfully produced InP QDs with exceptional crystallinity and stabil-
ity.  These  QDs  exhibited  small  particle  sizes,  tunable  within  the  range  of  2.5–3.7  nm, 
achieved by adjusting the reaction temperature between 300 and 430 °C. This temper-
ature  modulation  resulted  in  a  bandgap  tuning  range  of  approximately  0.4  eV  within 
the  visible  spectrum.  The  established  methodology  for  InP  QDs  synthesis  serves  as  a 
valuable  reference  for  fabricating  other  III-V  semiconductor  QDs.  Nozik  et  al.  further 
employed the solvothermal method to synthesize InP QDs with an average particle size 
of 2.5 ± 0.19 nm [51]. Yang et al. advanced this technique by developing a stepwise solvo-
thermal approach to synthesize highly fluorescent InP/ZnS core-shell QDs, achieving a 
remarkable fluorescence QY of 41–42%. Notably, the use of P(N(CH₃)₂)₃ as a precursor 
offers  significant  advantages  over  P(TMS)₃,  being  both  less  toxic  and  more  cost-effec-
tive, aligning with the principles of green chemistry and sustainable material synthesis 
[52]. Kuo et al.further demonstrated the potential of this approach by utilizing safe, eco-
friendly,  and  low-cost  precursors  to  synthesize  InP/ZnS  core-shell  QDs  with  tunable 
fluorescence  properties  through  the  green  solvothermal  method,  achieving  an  impres-
sive fluorescence QY of 60.1% [53].Thus, the solvothermal method shows potential in the 
controlled synthesis and green improvement of InP QDs, but its harsh synthesis condi-
tions, inherent defect control problems and scale-up barriers are still the core barriers to 
industrialization.  In  the  future,  synergistic  breakthroughs  in  performance  and  sustain-
ability should be realized through reaction path innovation, precise structure regulation 
and green process iteration.

3.1.2  Heating method for the preparation of inp QDs

The heating method is a reliable and scalable technique for colloidal nanocrystal synthe-
sis, which enables controlled nucleation and crystal growth by dissolving precursors and 
ligands in solvents and initiating reactions by heating. By optimizing the precursors, sta-
bilizers and heating rate, high quality nanocrystals comparable to thermal injection can 
be produced. However, the decomposition of ligands (e.g., oleylamine) at high tempera-
tures releases amine gases that irritate the respiratory tract. These gases participate in 
photochemical reactions to form secondary pollutants such as ozone. Rapid nucleation 
is also prone to causing lattice distortion and high defect densities in QDs. To mitigate 
environmental impact, solvents (e.g., octadecene, oleylamine) can be recovered via dis-
tillation or adsorption techniques, enabling closed-loop production. Figure 4a illustrates 
the fundamental process of nanocrystal formation in heated synthesis and its correlation 
with the reaction vessel temperature [54]. Pidluzhna et al. employed the heating method 
to  prepare  core-shell  InP/ZnS  hybrid  QDs,  as  depicted  in  Fig.  4b  Their  study  focused

rication  of  inverted  solar  cells,  utilizing  a  combination  of  thermal  vacuum  deposition 
and spin-coating techniques [55]. Wang et al. developed cadmium-free InP/ZnSeS/ZnS 
thick-shell QDs using the heating method. By varying the number of zinc sources, they 
controlled the emission wavelength of the InP core and optimized the thickness of the 
ZnS layer, thereby enhancing the quality of the QDs [56]. Kim et al. reported a simple 
one-pot heating method for synthesizing InP and InP/ZnS core-shell QDs. By precisely 
controlling the flow rate and crystal growth temperature, they successfully synthesized 
high-quality  InP/ZnS  QDs  with  tunable  emission  wavelengths  ranging  from  blue-
green to red [57].Summarizing, the heating method in the synthesis of InP-based QDs 
exhibits the advantages of controllable core-shell structure construction, precise emis-
sion  wavelength  tuning,  and  highly  efficient  synthesis  in  a  one-pot  method.  However, 
the limitations such as unresolved environmental risks, insufficient defects control, and 
poor process scalability are generally present. In the future, further breakthroughs can 
be achieved by developing bio-based ligands to replace oleylamine and coupling distilla-
tion/adsorption to achieve closed-loop production, introducing gradient shell layers and 
post-processing passivation to reduce the defect density, as well as combining microflu-
idic continuous-flow synthesis with machine-learning optimization of parameters.

3.1.3  Hot injection method for the preparation of inp QDs

The  hot-injection  method  achieves  the  separation  of  nucleation  and  growth  phases  by 
dissolving  the  precursor  in  organic  solvents  (e.g.,  octadecene,  oleylamine,  and  trioc-
tylphosphine) by heating and injecting another precursor several times at a specific tem-
perature  to  trigger  the  transient  supersaturation  of  the  solution,  which  allows  for  the 
homogeneous nucleation and controlled growth of crystals, and the products are both 
monodispersed and homogeneous; the variety of the choice of the reaction solvents and 
active  agents  further  expand  the  product  system  [34–58].  However,  the  volatilization/
decomposition of solvents at high temperatures (> 300 °C) releases volatile organic com-
pounds (VOCs) (amines, alkanes, etc.), which causes air pollution and health risks, and 
requires secondary treatment of the exhaust gases and waste liquids. For example, Jam-
shidi  Zavaraki  et  al.  employed  a  hot  injection  method  to  synthesize  colloidal  InP  and 
ZnS-covered InP QDs, which were successfully applied for the first time as sensitizers 
in quantum dot-sensitized solar cells (QDSSCs) [59]. However, the stability of colloidal

in this work to enhance the stability of InP and to protect InP QDs from moisture and 
interaction with electrolytes. Song et al. first introduced of high-quality InP QDs by the 
reaction of P(N(CH3)2)3 hot injected at 220 °C with In and Zn chlorides dissolved in the 
relatively weakly coordinated solvent oleylamine, and achieved an unprecedented series 
of controlled synthesis of bandgap-tunable InP QDs, successfully achieving nucleation/
growth of QDs (Fig. 5) [60]. Ramasamy et al. prepared InP/ZnS core-shell QDs using the 
hot injection method, and in this experiment, it was found that the presence of a small 
amount of water as an impurity not only significantly reduced the FWHM and increased 
the QY of InP/ZnS QDs [61]. InP/ZnS QDs obtained using In precursors and the pres-
ence of water in the solvent had a narrow FWHM of 46 nm and a high QY of 45%. In 
comparison, without water doping, the emission wavelength of the synthesized QDs was 
around 625 nm, with a FWHM of 66 nm and a QY of about 33% (its High Resolution 
Transmission Electron Microscope (HR-TEM) schematic of QDs synthesized with and 
without water was displayed in Fig. 6). Singh et al. successfully synthesized InP QDs and 
InP/ZnS core-shell structures using the hot injection technique. It was observed that the 
PL intensity increased gradually when the ZnS shell layer was increased, and the synthe-
sized QDs were treated with HF to remove the defects on the surface of QDs and thus 
enhanced the luminescence intensity [62]. Hot injection method shows multiple break-
throughs in the synthesis of InP QDs. However, the method still suffers from limitations 
such as high-temperature decomposition of solvents, unidentified mechanism of water 
impurity  enhancement,  and  strong  corrosive  waste  liquid  from  strong  acid  treatment. 
In the future, we need to focus on the development of low-toxicity solvents to replace 
oleylamine,  establish  a  quantitative  model  of  water  content  and  defect  states  to  stabi-
lize the process, and explore green defect passivation techniques such as photo/thermal 
annealing.

In  addition  to  the  aforementioned  common  preparation  methods,  alternative 
approaches such as ion exchange and crystal growth techniques, have been developed.

3.2  Graphene QDs

As  an  emerging  eco-friendly  nanomaterial,  GQDs,  with  their  unique  physicochemical 
properties,  such  as  high  specific  surface  area  (300–600  m2/g),  excellent  optical  prop-
erties,  such  as  strong  fluorescence  properties,  tunable  fluorescence,  and  high  optical 
absorption  from  UV  to  IR  (  [70].  And  superior  electrical  properties,  such  as  high  car-
rier  mobility  with  a  mobility  of  more  than  15000  cm²  V− 1  S− 1  [71],  tunable  energy  gap 
(2  eV  − 0.02  eV)  (  [72].  And  favorable  biocompatibility,  enable  them  to  play  an  impor-
tant role in the fields of efficient water treatment and pollution control, air purification 
and greenhouse gas control, clean energy development and energy storage, eco-friendly 
materials  and  biodegradable  technology,  environmental  monitoring  and  sensor,  etc.  (( 
[73–74]).  GQDs  not  only  possess  a  series  of  excellent  properties  of  graphene,  but  also 
combine the small size and quantum-limited domain effect of QDs at the same time. The 
height range of GQDs is usually between 0.4 and 4 nm, and the thickness is 2–4 nm, i.e., 
between  2-layer  and  4-layer  graphene  sheets.  The  lateral  dimensions  are  typically  less 
than 100 nm, with most studies focusing on the range of less than 10 nm. The number of 
graphene layers usually consists of 1–10 layers of graphene, with most not exceeding 5 
layers (( [75–76]). Therefore, the efficient preparation of GQDs is of great significance to

the development of human life. After years of development, the preparation methods of 
GQDs as a whole are divided into top-down and bottom-up synthesis methods.

3.2.1  Top-down method for the preparation of GQDs

The top-down approach allows direct physical or chemical access to large-area graphene 
arrays into GQDs with nanometer dimensions, controlling the shape, size, and growth 
direction of GQDs, and is suitable for large-scale production. However, the insufficient 
controllability of the size and shape of QDs prepared by this method, the serious surface 
defects and structural damages of QDs, the low efficiency of large-scale production, the 
high cost and energy consumption as well as the biocompatibility of nanoparticles limit 
their applications in medical fields. The top-down method presents diversified techno-
logical  paths  in  the  synthesis  of  GQDs,  such  as  Samra  et  al.  used  coke  as  a  raw  mate-
rial (with low impurities and high carbon content) to produce GQDs by a facile process 
(Fig.  9a),  and  spectroscopic  characterization  verified  the  feasibility  [77].  Xie  et  al.  syn-
thesized  highly  crystalline  monodispersed  bluish  N-GQDs  by  nitrogen-containing  3D 
nanocarbon electrochemical cutting (Fig. 9b), with a QY of 19.3% and nitrogen doping 
of 12.3%, combining both economic and green advantages [78]. Zhou’s team innovated 
acid vapor cutting of bulk nitrogen-doped carbon films (1 ml of nitric acid) and in situ 
filtration  to  obtain  water-soluble  blue-green  photoresponsive  N-GQDs  (1.5–3.7  nm, 
Fig.  10a),  circumventing  the  tedious  isolation  step  [79].  Tadyszak  et  al.  demonstrated 
that the that the graphene oxide precursor preparation of GOQDs did not change the 
C/O ratio, and found 500 nm strong fluorescence dispersion and paramagnetism under 
280–380 nm excitation (Fig. 10b) [80]. Soriano et al. developed GQDs fluorescence for 
the  detection  of  carbamates  in  water  by  using  mixed-acid  oxidation  to  modulate  the 
reaction time (Fig. 10c) [81].However, there are core limitations of this method, such as 
the strong corrosive waste liquid generated by the acid treatment method, the still low 
QY (< 20%) and the unclear mechanism of magnetic/optical property regulation. In the 
future, it could be attempted to develop green stripping technologies like laser/plasma to 
replace the strong acid process, construct doping-fluorescence-magnetism constitutive 
relationship models, and explore biomass carbon sources to reduce costs and increase 
efficiency.

3.2.2  Bottom-up Preparation method for the Preparation of GQDs

The  bottom-up  approach  is  to  synthesize  GQDs  organically  by  the  carbonization  of 
organic  molecules  (e.g.,  citric  acid,  glucose,  etc.)  or  polymers  (the  process  is  depicted 
in Fig. 11). The advantage of this method is that it is easy to control the shape and size 
of GQDs, which is an irreplaceable advantage in regulating the physical properties and 
molecular structure of substances. There are also certain disadvantages, such as the syn-
thesis of large-size GQDs with many steps and cumbersome processes [82]. Prof. Chi-
ang’s  team  investigated  a  bottom-up  preparation  method  for  the  synthesis  of  colloidal 
QDs  using  an  aqueous  organosulfate  solution  treated  with  an  atmospheric  pressure 
argon  (Ar)  microplasma  [83].  The  average  diameter  of  the  fabricated  colloidal  GQDs 
was 4.9 nm, the QY was 1.5%, and the room temperature photoluminescence peak was 
448  nm.  Xu  et  al.used  a  top-down  preparation  method  to  synthesize  GQDs  with  high 
solubility  and  excellent  film-forming  ability  in  common  organic  solvents.  Significantly, 
this research not only solved the limitation of low solubility of GQDs prepared by tra-
ditional methods in organic solubility but also expected to successfully apply GQDs in 
other  optoelectronic  fields  [84].Gao’s  team  applied  a  bottom-up  synthesis  method  to

3.3  CuInS2 QDs

CuInS₂ QDs (CIS QDs) have emerged as an ideal alternative to traditional Cd/Pb-con-
taining QDs due to their prominent advantages, including environmental benignity, low 
toxicity (compliant with international environmental regulations such as the EU RoHS 
directive), broad spectral tunability (excellent solar spectrum matching with adjustable 
emission  ranging  from  500  to  800  nm  and  QY  up  to  80%),  exceptional  photostability 
and chemical robustness (manifested in superior photobleaching resistance and stabil-
ity under oxidative/acid-base environments), as well as cost-effectiveness and abundant 
elemental availability [86–88]. These distinctive characteristics render them a promising 
candidate  for  diverse  applications  spanning  biomedical  engineering,  renewable  energy 
technologies, and advanced display systems. However, the development of ternary CIS 
QDs  still  faces  several  challenges,  including  low  charge  injection  efficiency,  exciton 
quenching induced by interfacial space charge accumulation between charge transport 
layers, and interlayer miscibility during spin-coating processes [87–89]. Recent advance-
ments  in  core-shell  engineering  and  surface  chemistry  hold  promise  for  overcoming 
these  performance  limitations,  thereby  accelerating  the  practical  implementation  of 
green  nanotechnology.  The  following  sections  comprehensively  review  several  simple 
yet efficient synthesis strategies for CIS QDs.

3.3.1  Hot injection method for the Preparation of CIS QDs

In the study of the synthesis of CIS QDs, hot injection is an effective means of preparing 
high-quality  monodisperse  QDs,  but  is  limited  by  the  scarcity  of  low-toxicity  or  non-
toxic precursors. Zhu et al. applied a low-temperature hot injection preparation method 
to synthesize super-efficient green luminescent CIS QDs (the synthesis process appeared 
in Fig. 12). The introduction of S- Oil Amine (OAm)(S powder dissolved in ethylamine)

3.3.2  Cation exchange and template synthesis for the preparation of CIS QDs

Cation  exchange,  as  an  efficient  two-stage  synthesis  strategy,  has  become  a  key  tech-

5  Conclusion

Under globally tightening environmental regulations such as the RoHS Directive and the 
WEEE  Directive,  eco-friendly  QDs  including  InP,  graphene,  and  CuInS₂  are  poised  to 
revolutionize  biomedical,  optoelectronic  sensing,  display,  and  energy-efficient  lighting 
industries. The innovation and advancement of these QDs align with the United Nations 
Sustainable  Development  Goals  (SDGs)  and  national  green  manufacturing  policies, 
establishing  regulatory  prerequisites  for  cross-industrial  adoption  of  environmentally 
compliant  nanomaterials.  Eco-friendly  QDs  exhibit  distinct  technological  advantages. 
For instance, InP QDs demonstrate tunable bandgaps (emission sizes of 2.5–3.7 nm) and 

He et al. Discover Nano          (2025) 20:132  
 Page 35 of 40

near-commercial  external  quantum  efficiency  (EQE > 15%  in  QLEDs),  thus  positioning 
them  as  RoHS-compliant  alternatives  for  next-generation  displays.  Graphene-derived 
QDs meet ISO 10,993 biocompatibility standards with cytotoxicity below 5% and mul-
timodal  imaging  capabilities.  Meanwhile,  CIS  QDs  achieve  60.1%  PLQY  using  low-
toxicity  precursors,  reducing  hazardous  waste  by  80%  compared  to  conventional  Cd/
Pb-based QDs synthesis. Since 2022, twelve eco-friendly QDs products have been certi-
fied under China’s GB/T 26,572 − 2021 standard. However, challenges persist in develop-
ing green QDs, such as QDs fluorescence imaging exhibits low sensitivity in deep-tissue 
in  vivo  applications,  while  metal-organic  chemical  synthesis  of  QD  nanocrystals  faces 
stringent  synthesis  conditions,  complex  reaction  protocols,  high  costs,  and  abundant 
surface defects.

6  Prospect

In the foreseeable future, with the continuous breakthroughs in eco-friendly QDs prepa-
ration technologies such as biological template synthesis and microwave-assisted prepa-
ration, coupled with the market forces driven by government green industry subsidies, 
environmental tax incentives, and other policies, the interplay and synergy of these two 
factors will strongly promote a profound transformation of the research paradigm in the 
field  of  nanotechnology. The  in-depth  exploration  of  cutting-edge  theories  by  the  aca-
demic community, the urgent need for technology transfer in the industrial sector, and 
the goal of policymakers to create a favorable development environment make strategic 
cooperation among the three parties the key to overcoming technical bottlenecks such 
as insufficient stability of QDs and difficulties in large-scale production. Specifically, by 
actively advancing the refinement of core-shell engineering to enhance the performance 
of QDs, deeply integrating the concept of circular economy to achieve efficient resource 
utilization  and  minimize  waste,  and  simultaneously  accelerating  the  unification  and 
standardization of regulatory standards, it is promising to establish a green and sustain-
able  nanotechnology  ecosystem.  This  ecosystem  will  not  only  strictly  comply  with  the 
increasingly stringent global environmental requirements but also bring transformative 
industrial applications to fields such as optoelectronic devices and biomedical imaging, 
reshaping  the  relevant  industrial  landscape  and  propelling  global  science,  technology, 
and industry towards a greener and more efficient future.

3.1.1  Solvothermal preparation of inp QDs

The  solvothermal  method  represents  an  efficient  and  rapid  approach  for  synthesizing 
highly  crystalline  and  monodisperse  InP  QDs.  This  synthetic  route  involves  the  intro-
duction of precursor mixtures into a solvent maintained at a specific temperature under 
an inert gas atmosphere, facilitating the instantaneous crystallization of InP monomers 
into core structures. This method offers precise control over QDs size, thereby enabling 
effective  bandgap  engineering.  However,  the  method  requires  high  temperature  and 
Pressure confined system (usually > 300 °C, > 10 MPa), which increases the risk of explo-
sion and the difficulty of safe operation. And its solvent and precursor toxicity will cause 
a certain burden on the environment. As demonstrated by Sarma et al., the solvothermal 
synthesis route successfully produced InP QDs with exceptional crystallinity and stabil-
ity.  These  QDs  exhibited  small  particle  sizes,  tunable  within  the  range  of  2.5–3.7  nm, 
achieved by adjusting the reaction temperature between 300 and 430 °C. This temper-
ature  modulation  resulted  in  a  bandgap  tuning  range  of  approximately  0.4  eV  within 
the  visible  spectrum.  The  established  methodology  for  InP  QDs  synthesis  serves  as  a 
valuable  reference  for  fabricating  other  III-V  semiconductor  QDs.  Nozik  et  al.  further 
employed the solvothermal method to synthesize InP QDs with an average particle size 
of 2.5 ± 0.19 nm [51]. Yang et al. advanced this technique by developing a stepwise solvo-
thermal approach to synthesize highly fluorescent InP/ZnS core-shell QDs, achieving a 
remarkable fluorescence QY of 41–42%. Notably, the use of P(N(CH₃)₂)₃ as a precursor 
offers  significant  advantages  over  P(TMS)₃,  being  both  less  toxic  and  more  cost-effec-

[52]. Kuo et al.further demonstrated the potential of this approach by utilizing safe, eco-

fluorescence  properties  through  the  green  solvothermal  method,  achieving  an  impres-
sive fluorescence QY of 60.1% [53].Thus, the solvothermal method shows potential in the 
controlled synthesis and green improvement of InP QDs, but its harsh synthesis condi-
tions, inherent defect control problems and scale-up barriers are still the core barriers to 
industrialization.  In  the  future,  synergistic  breakthroughs  in  performance  and  sustain-

3.3  CuInS2 QDs

CuInS₂ QDs (CIS QDs) have emerged as an ideal alternative to traditional Cd/Pb-con-
taining QDs due to their prominent advantages, including environmental benignity, low 
toxicity (compliant with international environmental regulations such as the EU RoHS 
directive), broad spectral tunability (excellent solar spectrum matching with adjustable 
emission  ranging  from  500  to  800  nm  and  QY  up  to  80%),  exceptional  photostability

these  performance  limitations,  thereby  accelerating  the  practical  implementation  of

yet efficient synthesis strategies for CIS QDs.

5  Conclusion

Under globally tightening environmental regulations such as the RoHS Directive and the 
WEEE  Directive,  eco-friendly  QDs  including  InP,  graphene,  and  CuInS₂  are  poised  to 
revolutionize  biomedical,  optoelectronic  sensing,  display,  and  energy-efficient  lighting 
industries. The innovation and advancement of these QDs align with the United Nations 
Sustainable  Development  Goals  (SDGs)  and  national  green  manufacturing  policies, 
establishing  regulatory  prerequisites  for  cross-industrial  adoption  of  environmentally 
compliant  nanomaterials.  Eco-friendly  QDs  exhibit  distinct  technological  advantages. 
For instance, InP QDs demonstrate tunable bandgaps (emission sizes of 2.5–3.7 nm) and

near-commercial  external  quantum  efficiency  (EQE > 15%  in  QLEDs),  thus  positioning 
them  as  RoHS-compliant  alternatives  for  next-generation  displays.  Graphene-derived 
QDs meet ISO 10,993 biocompatibility standards with cytotoxicity below 5% and mul-
timodal  imaging  capabilities.  Meanwhile,  CIS  QDs  achieve  60.1%  PLQY  using  low-
toxicity  precursors,  reducing  hazardous  waste  by  80%  compared  to  conventional  Cd/
Pb-based QDs synthesis. Since 2022, twelve eco-friendly QDs products have been certi-
fied under China’s GB/T 26,572 − 2021 standard. However, challenges persist in develop-
ing green QDs, such as QDs fluorescence imaging exhibits low sensitivity in deep-tissue 
in  vivo  applications,  while  metal-organic  chemical  synthesis  of  QD  nanocrystals  faces 
stringent  synthesis  conditions,  complex  reaction  protocols,  high  costs,  and  abundant 
surface defects.

6  Prospect

In the foreseeable future, with the continuous breakthroughs in eco-friendly QDs prepa-
ration technologies such as biological template synthesis and microwave-assisted prepa-
ration, coupled with the market forces driven by government green industry subsidies, 
environmental tax incentives, and other policies, the interplay and synergy of these two 
factors will strongly promote a profound transformation of the research paradigm in the 
field  of  nanotechnology. The  in-depth  exploration  of  cutting-edge  theories  by  the  aca-
demic community, the urgent need for technology transfer in the industrial sector, and 
the goal of policymakers to create a favorable development environment make strategic 
cooperation among the three parties the key to overcoming technical bottlenecks such 
as insufficient stability of QDs and difficulties in large-scale production. Specifically, by 
actively advancing the refinement of core-shell engineering to enhance the performance 
of QDs, deeply integrating the concept of circular economy to achieve efficient resource 
utilization  and  minimize  waste,  and  simultaneously  accelerating  the  unification  and 
standardization of regulatory standards, it is promising to establish a green and sustain-
able  nanotechnology  ecosystem.  This  ecosystem  will  not  only  strictly  comply  with  the 
increasingly stringent global environmental requirements but also bring transformative 
industrial applications to fields such as optoelectronic devices and biomedical imaging, 
reshaping  the  relevant  industrial  landscape  and  propelling  global  science,  technology, 
and industry towards a greener and more efficient future.

Abstract
Semiconductor Quantum-dots (QDs), characterized by their unique optoelectronic 
tunability, high efficiency, and multifunctionality, have emerged as transformative 
materials in diverse fields, including display technologies, energy conversion, 
solar cells, biomedical applications, and quantum technologies. With ongoing 
advancements in material synthesis and device engineering, the application scope of 
QDs is anticipated to expand further, thereby driving interdisciplinary technological 
innovations and fostering breakthroughs across multiple scientific fields. However, 
in recent years, the rapid development of Cd, Pb, and Hg-based QDs has raised 
significant environmental and biological concerns due to the inherent toxicity of 
these heavy metals. Consequently, these materials have been classified as restricted 
substances by major global entities, including international organizations, the 
European Union, and the United States, through international treaties and domestic 
legislation. To mitigate legal risks associated with environmental pollution, the 
development of non-toxic and environmentally friendly (eco-friendly) QDs has 
become imperative. This review focuses on several eco-friendly QDs, such as indium 
phosphide (InP), copper indium sulfide (CuInS₂), and graphene QDs (GQDs), from 
the perspective of environmental compliance. It comprehensively discusses their 
synthesis methods, application domains, and the advantages and disadvantages of 
different preparation techniques, along with their environmental impacts. Finally, the 
review summarizes the existing challenges, limitations, and potential solutions for the 
development of environmentally benign QDs.

Keywords  Environmental compliance, Eco-friendly QDs, InP QDs, CuInS₂ QDs, 
Graphene QDs

1  Introduction

QDs  technology’s  impact  has  exceeded  mere  technological  advances  and  is  reinvent-
ing human lifestyles, economic models, and even civilization. In 1983, Brus et al. at Bell 
Laboratories  first  reported  the  quantum  size  effect  in  CdS  nanocrystals,  marking  the

inception of QDs research [1]. QDs is quasi-zero-dimensional semiconductor nanocrys-
tals consisting  of a small  number of atoms that bind excitons in H-dimensional space, 
with a radius generally smaller than or close to the exciton bolometric radius, between 
1  and  10  nm.  The  electronic  structure  exhibits  a  unique  set  of  optoelectronic  proper-
ties due to the change from a continuous energy level structure to a quasi-split energy 
level, i.e., with quantum-limited effects [2–4]. As (1) QDs can be tuned in size or struc-
tural  composition,  leading  to  spectral  emission  in  the  entire  visible  region  [5–6].  (2) 
with a broad excitation spectrum and narrow emission spectrum, and its full width at 
half  maximum  (FWHM)  is  narrow  [7–8].  (3)  Excellent  photostability  [9–11].  (4)  Long 
fluorescence lifetime, surface chemical plasticity, and good biocompatibility [12–13]. In 
addition,  semiconductor  colloidal  QDs  also  have  excellent  properties  such  as  solution 
processability and high color purity [14].

Currently,  researchers  have  established  a  variety  of  mechanisms  for  QDs  synthesis, 
which are divided into two main categories, namely physical preparation methods and 
chemical  preparation  methods  [15–19].  The  most  common  is  chemical  preparation, 
which is divided into two main methods: one is organic synthesis, and the other is syn-
thesis in the aqueous phase [20–22]. Organic synthesis of QDs employs organometallic 
precursors (e.g., Cd(CH3)2, Zn(CH3)2), which are highly unstable, sensitive to water and 
oxygen, toxic, flammable, and explosive, and the preparation process can only be carried 
out in a glove box filled with nitrogen. The process is complex and not suitable for large-
scale production. Comparatively, the aqueous-phase synthesis is simple to operate and 
have  a  low  cost.  It  requires  no  further  modification,  and  QDs  such  as  CdS,  CdSe,  and 
ZnSe have been successfully obtained in aqueous solution [23–26]. QDs has a high spe-
cific surface area with undercoordinated surface atoms, leading to pronounced surface 
defects  that  facilitate  atomic  aggregation  and  agglomeration,  resulting  in  poor  optical 
properties  of  QDs  [27].  Over  the  years,  researchers  have  made  many  efforts  to  elimi-
nate the surface defects of QDs, the most common of which is to modify the surface of 
QDs  using  various  organic  and  inorganic  materials. The  surface  modification  of  semi-
conductor fluorescent QDs mainly includes inorganic shell layer passivation surface and 
functionalized group modification surface. For instance, Hines and Guyot-Sionnes first 
proposed to wrap 1–2 monolayers of ZnS shell layers on top of CdSe nanocrystals with a 
particle size of 3 nm, and eventually the quantum yield (QY) of QDs based on the CdSe/
ZnS core-shell structure was enhanced to 50% [28]. Murcia et al. used acoustic chemis-
try driven synthesis of CdSe QDs and subsequently coated ZnS on the surface of CdSe 
QDs  also  by  acoustic  chemistry  driven,  with  a  QY  of  50%-60%  and  FWHM  of  25  nm 
[29]. Roy et al. reported a microwave-assisted synthesis of water-soluble CdSe/ZnS QDs 
with a maximum emission wavelength of 511 nm to 596 nm [30]. Functionalized groups 
modifying the surface of QDs commonly include organic small molecule modifications 
and organic polymer modifications, as Qian et al. combined experimental and theoreti-
cal approaches to systematically investigate the surface chemistry of a series of graphene 
QDs functionalized with small organic molecules. The surface functionalization of gra-
phene QDs with alcohols, amines and thiols can effectively modulate the fluorescence of 
graphene QDs, and demonstrate that amines can significantly improve the QY of modi-
fied graphene QDs [31].

As  shown  in  Figs.  1  and  2,  heavy  metals  in  Cd-based  QDs  may  be  relatively  harm-
ful  to  the  environment  and  living  organisms,  and  in  severe  cases  can  lead  to  serious

chronic  diseases  and  cancers  [32–33].  The  UN  Global  E-waste  Monitor  2024  reports 
that global electronic waste (e-waste) has surged to 62 million metric tons, with heavy 
metal emissions from this sector contributing 15–20% of the total industrial discharge. 
In response, multilateral environmental conventions have established a targeted gover-
nance framework, integrating legally binding protocols for toxic substance phase-outs. 
The Stockholm Declaration on the Human Environment (1972) establishes foundational 
environmental rights and obligations under Principle 1: “Humankind bears the solemn 
duty to preserve intergenerational ecological integrity, entitling all to a healthy environ-
ment while mandating stewardship for future generations.” Principle 21 further codifies 
state  responsibility  to  “prevent  transboundary  environmental  harm  through  toxic  sub-
stance  control.”  In  accordance  with  this  framework,  the  Rio  Declaration  on  Environ-
ment and Development (1992) articulates the “Precautionary Principle” in Principle 15: 
“Where  threats  of  serious  or  irreversible  damage  exist,  scientific  uncertainty  shall  not 
postpone cost-effective preventive measures, requiring states to implement anticipatory 
pollution controls through risk-weighted regulatory action and technology-forcing stan-
dards.”  The  Precautionary  Principle  prioritizes  early  intervention  through  legal  norms 

He et al. Discover Nano          (2025) 20:132  
 
 Page 4 of 40

enacted by public authorities to mitigate potential harm at its source. The jurispruden-
tial  essence  of  the  precautionary  principle  is  enshrined  in  the  Gabčíkovo-Nagymaros 
Project judgment (1997) by the International Court of Justice (ICJ):“Vigilance and pre-
vention are non-derogable obligations in environmental governance, as ecological harm 
is  characterized  by  irreversibility  and  remediation  inherently  constrained  by  scientific 
and  technical  limitations. This  ruling underscores the imperative for anticipatory legal 
interventions, even amid epistemic uncertainty, to avert systemic risks posed by persis-
tent pollutants.1 For QDs not to cause harmful results in terms of environmental pollu-
tion, legal norms must actively take measures to prevent such damage and must ensure 
that these measures are effectively implemented, which is an environmental compliance 
obligation. The development of eco-friendly QD synthesis technologies aligns with green 
chemistry principles and fulfills the environmental compliance requirements of the pre-
cautionary principle.

To date, eco-friendly QDs such as Indium Phosphide (InP) [34–35], graphene [36–37], 
CuInS2 [38–39], Zn-based, etc., have also been developed to a large extent. For instance, 
InP  QDs  has  superior  features  such  as  a  larger  exciton  wave  radius  and  high  carrier 
mobility,  stronger  quantum  confinement  effect,  wide  spectral  tunability,  and  larger 
intrinsic absorption coefficient, making them one of the excellent alternative materials 
for Cd-based QDs [40–41]. Yet, InP QDs also suffer from poor electron-binding ability, 
weak performance stability, and low QY. Graphene QDs, a new star in the family of car-
bon-based fluorescent nanomaterials, have received extensive attention from research-
ers  globally  in  recent  years  [42].  Graphene  QDs  possess  high  chemical  stability,  upper 
fluorescence  QY,  strong  resistance  to  photobleaching,  lower  cytotoxicity,  and  good 
biocompatibility.  In  addition,  they  also  have  significant  photoluminescence  properties, 
and fluorescence spectra with different emission wavelengths from the deep UV region 
to the IR region band can be obtained by changing the raw material ratios or synthesis 
pathways [43–44]. However, graphene QDs also often have broad emission peaks due to 
defective luminescence as well as poor carrier injection and low luminescence efficiency, 
limiting their more profound development in the field of illumination [45–47].

This paper first provides a comprehensive review of global regulatory frameworks gov-
erning heavy metal contaminants, particularly Cd, Hg, and Pb, with a focus on environ-
mental  compliance  requirements  in  key  jurisdictions,  including  the  United  States,  the 
European Union, China, and Japan. The examination encompassed five critical dimen-
sions: hazardous waste management protocols, production/usage restrictions, emission 
control  standards,  occupational  safety  regulations,  and  public  right-to-know  obliga-
tions. These legislative initiatives aim to mitigate heavy metal pollution through source 
control  and  exposure  minimization,  thereby  directly  driving  the  advancement  of  eco-
friendly quantum dot alternatives. Building on global regulatory frameworks, this study 
analyzes three eco-friendly QDs—InP QDs, graphene QDs, and ternary CuInS2 QDs by 
comparing  their  synthesis  methods  (hot  injection,  solvothermal,  and  thermal  decom-
position) and applications in optoelectronics, biomedicine, and environmental sensing. 
The  analysis  highlighted  critical  challenges:  QY  limitations  (> 35%  energy  loss),  ambi-
ent stability issues, and scalability constraints (± 15% batch variability). To address these 
issues,  we  propose  machine-learning-optimized  synthesis,  atomic-layer  encapsulation,

and  microfluidic  production,  ultimately  envisioning  hybrid  architectures  via  plasma-
enhanced doping to achieve > 95% quantum efficiency.

2  International and National regulatory frameworks governing heavy metal 
containment in QDs
2.1  International convention

The elimination of Cd, Pd, Hg, and their toxic and hazardous compounds at the sources 
of  production,  storage,  trade,  and  transfer  has  been  universally  recognized  in  the  for-
mulation  of  many  international  conventions.  An  international  convention  is  a  writ-
ten agreement between subjects of international law on mutual rights and obligations, 
which reflects the common will and interests of state parties [48]. As the development 
of  international  environmental  issues  will  ultimately  affect  the  alteration  of  the  entire 
Earth’s  ecosystem,  their  outcome  is  closely  linked  to  the  survival  of  human  beings  on 
Earth. In addition, emerging international environmental problems, such as holes in the 
ozone layer and transboundary waste transfer, cannot be solved by a single country and 
need to be regulated by multilateral international conventions of a global and regional 
nature  [49].  As  delineated  in  Fig.  3,  five  pivotal  conventions  (Basel,  Rotterdam,  Stock-
holm, Bamako, and Minamata) form the BRS + governance architecture. These regimes 
aim to collectively address the global challenges of heavy metal management by harmo-
nizing standards to control the transboundary movement of hazardous substances and 
their impacts on human health and the environment.

Non-compliant  states  primarily  risk  reputational  damage  or  trade  privilege  revoca-
tion  rather  than  coercive  penalties,  as  evidenced  by  persistent  non-compliance  with 
the  Stockholm  Convention  mandates  on  toxic  substance  phase-outs,  where  Cd-based 
QDs  remain  prevalent  because  of  economic  prioritization  and  technological  path 
dependencies. For example, the Minamata Convention’s decade-long adoption timeline

exemplifies how conflicting national interests (e.g., differentiated emission responsibili-
ties between industrialized and developing economies) protract multilateral consensus

2.2  2.2 National legislation

National legislation on heavy metal contaminants (Cd, Hg, Pb) emphasizes source con-
trol  through  production  bans  and  import  restrictions.  As  delineated  in  Table  1,  the 
United States implements prior informed consent (PIC) protocols, mandating dual obli-
gations:  exporter  disclosure  of  chemical  profiles  for  specified  imports  and  consumer 
notification requirements for toxic substance-containing products. In contrast, the EU 
adopts preventative measures by limiting heavy metal concentrations in electronics and 
batteries while incentivizing safer alternatives through Horizon Europe funding mecha-
nisms. Major economies, including China, Japan, and South Korea, operationalize three-
phase regulatory models: (i) formal classification of Cd/Pb/Hg compounds as hazardous 
substances,  (ii)  manufacturing  prohibitions  coupled  with  product  toxicity  thresholds, 
and  (iii)  import  control  regimes  targeting  non-compliant  goods.  These  frameworks 
demonstrate  regulatory  convergence  in  life-cycle  management  of  toxic  metals  despite 
jurisdictional variations in implementation timelines.

Consequently,  this  regulatory  landscape  has  catalyzed  substantial  innovations  across 
multiple  domains,  including  the  development  of  toxic  metal  alternatives,  optimization 
of synthesis processes, and implementation of comprehensive risk mitigation strategies. 
This transformative shift represents a convergence of regulatory alignment and sustain-
able material science innovation, marking a new era in nanomaterial development and 
application [50].

3  Eco-friendly QDs from an environmental compliance perspective

With  the  enhancement  of  environmental  awareness  and  the  increasing  strictness  of 
environmental  regulations,  various  industries  are  undergoing  a  transformation  toward 
sustainable  development. The  development  of  eco-friendly  QDs  aligns  with  this  trend, 
contributing to the sustainable development of quantum dot-related industries. By meet-
ing market demands for the optical properties of quantum dot materials while reducing 
environmental  impacts,  it  achieves  a  harmonious  integration  of  economic  growth  and 
environmental  protection.  The  advancement  of  eco-friendly  QDs  can  drive  the  entire 
quantum dot industry to transition toward green and environmentally friendly practices, 
prompting  relevant  enterprises  to  research,  develop,  and  adopt  more  sustainable  pro-
duction processes and materials. This encourages collaborative efforts across the entire 
industrial  chain  to  improve  resource  utilization  efficiency,  reduce  pollutant  emissions, 
and  enhance  the  overall  environmental  performance  of  the  industry,  thereby  better 
addressing the challenges posed by increasingly stringent environmental regulations and 
market  demands  for  eco-friendly  products.Therefore,  this  section  mainly  summarizes

environmental protection requirements for the development of QDs in modern society.

3.1.1  Solvothermal preparation of inp QDs

The  solvothermal  method  represents  an  efficient  and  rapid  approach  for  synthesizing 
highly  crystalline  and  monodisperse  InP  QDs.  This  synthetic  route  involves  the  intro-
duction of precursor mixtures into a solvent maintained at a specific temperature under 
an inert gas atmosphere, facilitating the instantaneous crystallization of InP monomers 
into core structures. This method offers precise control over QDs size, thereby enabling 
effective  bandgap  engineering.  However,  the  method  requires  high  temperature  and 
Pressure confined system (usually > 300 °C, > 10 MPa), which increases the risk of explo-
sion and the difficulty of safe operation. And its solvent and precursor toxicity will cause 
a certain burden on the environment. As demonstrated by Sarma et al., the solvothermal 
synthesis route successfully produced InP QDs with exceptional crystallinity and stabil-
ity.  These  QDs  exhibited  small  particle  sizes,  tunable  within  the  range  of  2.5–3.7  nm, 
achieved by adjusting the reaction temperature between 300 and 430 °C. This temper-
ature  modulation  resulted  in  a  bandgap  tuning  range  of  approximately  0.4  eV  within 
the  visible  spectrum.  The  established  methodology  for  InP  QDs  synthesis  serves  as  a 
valuable  reference  for  fabricating  other  III-V  semiconductor  QDs.  Nozik  et  al.  further 
employed the solvothermal method to synthesize InP QDs with an average particle size 
of 2.5 ± 0.19 nm [51]. Yang et al. advanced this technique by developing a stepwise solvo-
thermal approach to synthesize highly fluorescent InP/ZnS core-shell QDs, achieving a 
remarkable fluorescence QY of 41–42%. Notably, the use of P(N(CH₃)₂)₃ as a precursor 
offers  significant  advantages  over  P(TMS)₃,  being  both  less  toxic  and  more  cost-effec-
tive, aligning with the principles of green chemistry and sustainable material synthesis 
[52]. Kuo et al.further demonstrated the potential of this approach by utilizing safe, eco-
friendly,  and  low-cost  precursors  to  synthesize  InP/ZnS  core-shell  QDs  with  tunable 
fluorescence  properties  through  the  green  solvothermal  method,  achieving  an  impres-
sive fluorescence QY of 60.1% [53].Thus, the solvothermal method shows potential in the 
controlled synthesis and green improvement of InP QDs, but its harsh synthesis condi-
tions, inherent defect control problems and scale-up barriers are still the core barriers to 
industrialization.  In  the  future,  synergistic  breakthroughs  in  performance  and  sustain-
ability should be realized through reaction path innovation, precise structure regulation 
and green process iteration.

ligands in solvents and initiating reactions by heating. By optimizing the precursors, sta-

3.1.3  Hot injection method for the preparation of inp QDs

The  hot-injection  method  achieves  the  separation  of  nucleation  and  growth  phases  by 
dissolving  the  precursor  in  organic  solvents  (e.g.,  octadecene,  oleylamine,  and  trioc-
tylphosphine) by heating and injecting another precursor several times at a specific tem-
perature  to  trigger  the  transient  supersaturation  of  the  solution,  which  allows  for  the 
homogeneous nucleation and controlled growth of crystals, and the products are both 
monodispersed and homogeneous; the variety of the choice of the reaction solvents and 
active  agents  further  expand  the  product  system  [34–58].  However,  the  volatilization/
decomposition of solvents at high temperatures (> 300 °C) releases volatile organic com-
pounds (VOCs) (amines, alkanes, etc.), which causes air pollution and health risks, and 
requires secondary treatment of the exhaust gases and waste liquids. For example, Jam-
shidi  Zavaraki  et  al.  employed  a  hot  injection  method  to  synthesize  colloidal  InP  and 
ZnS-covered InP QDs, which were successfully applied for the first time as sensitizers 
in quantum dot-sensitized solar cells (QDSSCs) [59]. However, the stability of colloidal

As  an  emerging  eco-friendly  nanomaterial,  GQDs,  with  their  unique  physicochemical

erties,  such  as  strong  fluorescence  properties,  tunable  fluorescence,  and  high  optical 
absorption  from  UV  to  IR  (  [70].  And  superior  electrical  properties,  such  as  high  car-

3.3  CuInS2 QDs

CuInS₂ QDs (CIS QDs) have emerged as an ideal alternative to traditional Cd/Pb-con-
taining QDs due to their prominent advantages, including environmental benignity, low 
toxicity (compliant with international environmental regulations such as the EU RoHS 
directive), broad spectral tunability (excellent solar spectrum matching with adjustable 
emission  ranging  from  500  to  800  nm  and  QY  up  to  80%),  exceptional  photostability 
and chemical robustness (manifested in superior photobleaching resistance and stabil-
ity under oxidative/acid-base environments), as well as cost-effectiveness and abundant 
elemental availability [86–88]. These distinctive characteristics render them a promising 
candidate  for  diverse  applications  spanning  biomedical  engineering,  renewable  energy 
technologies, and advanced display systems. However, the development of ternary CIS 
QDs  still  faces  several  challenges,  including  low  charge  injection  efficiency,  exciton 
quenching induced by interfacial space charge accumulation between charge transport 
layers, and interlayer miscibility during spin-coating processes [87–89]. Recent advance-
ments  in  core-shell  engineering  and  surface  chemistry  hold  promise  for  overcoming 
these  performance  limitations,  thereby  accelerating  the  practical  implementation  of 
green  nanotechnology.  The  following  sections  comprehensively  review  several  simple 
yet efficient synthesis strategies for CIS QDs.

4.3  Applications of CIS QDs in different fields

4.3.1  CIS QDs for solar cells applications

CIS-based QDs offer significant advantages in solar cells: their 1.5–1.8 eV energy band 
structure matches the solar spectrum for efficient capture of visible-near-infrared light. 
Excellent carrier transport properties promote rapid photogenerated charge separation, 
enhancing short-circuit current and fill factor. Environmental friendliness (heavy metal 
free)  and  low-cost  solution  method  preparation  (spin  coating/inkjet  printing)  support 
scale-up production. Fine tuning of size, composition, and surface ligands optimizes the 
energy level matching of optoelectronic devices, simultaneously enhancing performance 
and long-term operational reliability [139–140].

solar cells through interface engineering. For example, Konstantatos et al. used formic

4.3.2  CIS QDs for QLEDs applications

CIS  QDs  has  excellent  luminescence  performance  with  narrow  half-peak  width  (high 
color purity), adjustable light-emitting wavelengths (covering the visible range) and good 
QY, which enable high saturation and high contrast color displays, and their absorption 
and fluorescence spectra can be adjusted up to near-infrared wavelength bands. Com-
pared  to  conventional  cadmium-containing  QDs,  they  are  more  structurally  stable  in 
air and light conditions, contributing to the long-term operating life of QLEDs devices. 
The  HOMO/LUMO  energy  levels  can  be  optimized  by  adjusting  the  size  of  the  QDs, 
surface ligands, or alloying treatment, so as to achieve better interfacial matching with

cient  white  QLEDs  with  high  color  rendering  index  (CRI,  90)  and  4360  K  correlated 
color  temperature  [147].  Park  et  al.  introduced  CIS/ZnS/ZnS  QDs  and  showed  that

4.3.3  CIS QDs for sensing applications

Due  to  its  unique  physicochemical  properties,  CuInS2  QDs  exhibit  significant  applica-
tion potential  in  pressure sensing, biosensing and optical sensing. In pressure sensing, 
its  quantum-limited-domain  effect  confers  size-sensitive  optical  properties,  and  exter-
nal  pressure-induced  lattice  aberrations  can  be  precisely  monitored  by  fluorescence 
wavelength  or  intensity  changes.In  the  field  of  biosensing,  the  near-infrared  lumines-
cence  characteristics  of  the  QDs  make  them  strongly  penetrating  to  biological  tissues, 
while the advantages of poor self-absorption and minimal background noise can signifi-
cantly enhance the signal-to-noise ratio of in vivo imaging, which is especially suitable 
for the non-invasive detection of biomarkers in deep tissues. In optical sensing, multi-
parameter  response  optical  sensing  arrays  can  be  constructed  to  realize  super-selec-

resonance energy transfer or surface plasmon resonance mechanisms [150–151]. Safari

5  Conclusion

Under globally tightening environmental regulations such as the RoHS Directive and the 
WEEE  Directive,  eco-friendly  QDs  including  InP,  graphene,  and  CuInS₂  are  poised  to 
revolutionize  biomedical,  optoelectronic  sensing,  display,  and  energy-efficient  lighting 
industries. The innovation and advancement of these QDs align with the United Nations 
Sustainable  Development  Goals  (SDGs)  and  national  green  manufacturing  policies, 
establishing  regulatory  prerequisites  for  cross-industrial  adoption  of  environmentally 
compliant  nanomaterials.  Eco-friendly  QDs  exhibit  distinct  technological  advantages. 
For instance, InP QDs demonstrate tunable bandgaps (emission sizes of 2.5–3.7 nm) and

near-commercial  external  quantum  efficiency  (EQE > 15%  in  QLEDs),  thus  positioning 
them  as  RoHS-compliant  alternatives  for  next-generation  displays.  Graphene-derived 
QDs meet ISO 10,993 biocompatibility standards with cytotoxicity below 5% and mul-
timodal  imaging  capabilities.  Meanwhile,  CIS  QDs  achieve  60.1%  PLQY  using  low-
toxicity  precursors,  reducing  hazardous  waste  by  80%  compared  to  conventional  Cd/
Pb-based QDs synthesis. Since 2022, twelve eco-friendly QDs products have been certi-
fied under China’s GB/T 26,572 − 2021 standard. However, challenges persist in develop-
ing green QDs, such as QDs fluorescence imaging exhibits low sensitivity in deep-tissue 
in  vivo  applications,  while  metal-organic  chemical  synthesis  of  QD  nanocrystals  faces 
stringent  synthesis  conditions,  complex  reaction  protocols,  high  costs,  and  abundant 
surface defects.

6  Prospect

In the foreseeable future, with the continuous breakthroughs in eco-friendly QDs prepa-
ration technologies such as biological template synthesis and microwave-assisted prepa-
ration, coupled with the market forces driven by government green industry subsidies, 
environmental tax incentives, and other policies, the interplay and synergy of these two 
factors will strongly promote a profound transformation of the research paradigm in the 
field  of  nanotechnology. The  in-depth  exploration  of  cutting-edge  theories  by  the  aca-
demic community, the urgent need for technology transfer in the industrial sector, and 
the goal of policymakers to create a favorable development environment make strategic 
cooperation among the three parties the key to overcoming technical bottlenecks such 
as insufficient stability of QDs and difficulties in large-scale production. Specifically, by 
actively advancing the refinement of core-shell engineering to enhance the performance 
of QDs, deeply integrating the concept of circular economy to achieve efficient resource 
utilization  and  minimize  waste,  and  simultaneously  accelerating  the  unification  and 
standardization of regulatory standards, it is promising to establish a green and sustain-
able  nanotechnology  ecosystem.  This  ecosystem  will  not  only  strictly  comply  with  the 
increasingly stringent global environmental requirements but also bring transformative 
industrial applications to fields such as optoelectronic devices and biomedical imaging, 
reshaping  the  relevant  industrial  landscape  and  propelling  global  science,  technology, 
and industry towards a greener and more efficient future.
